ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The mass of the metal rod ab is $0.2\mathrm{kg}$, its length is $0.5\mathrm{m}$, and it carries a current of 1A. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field with a magnetic induction strength of 2T, where the direction of the magnetic field makes an angle $\boldsymbol{\Theta}\!=\!37^{\circ}$ with the plane of the rail. The conductor rod is exactly stationary. It is known that $\mathrm{g}\!=\!10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, $\sin37^{\circ}=0.6$, and $\cos37^{\circ}=0.8$.

1. Determine the coefficient of kinetic friction $\upmu$ between the conducting rod and the rails.
2. If all other conditions remain unchanged, reverse the magnetic field and gradually increase the magnetic induction intensity. When the conductor rod just begins to move, find the magnetic induction intensity $B$ at this moment (assuming the maximum static friction equals the sliding friction).

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure there are two parallel guide rails, and metal rod ab is placed obliquely and bridges between the upper and lower guide rails; beside the rod is labeled current i, indicating that the current passes along the direction of the oblique rod; on the left side is the power supply connected to the guide rails. In the figure, magnetic field B is represented by an arrow obliquely upward to the right, and its angle with the plane where the guide rails are located is marked as θ=37°. Reasoning: According to the problem statement and figure, use the right-hand rule to judge that under the initial magnetic field the Ampere force has a component along the direction of the guide rails, giving the rod a tendency to move; it also has a vertical component, directed upward, therefore it will reduce the pressure of the rod on the guide rails. Take the magnitude of the Ampere force as F=BIL. Initially B=2 T, I=1 A, L=0.5 m, so F=2×1×0.5=1 N. The component along the guide rails is F_parallel=BIL sinθ=1×0.6=0.6 N; the vertically upward component is F_vertical=BIL cosθ=1×0.8=0.8 N. The weight of the rod mg=0.2×10=2 N, so the support force N=mg-F_vertical=2-0.8=1.2 N. When the rod is just at rest, the Ampere force along the guide rails is balanced by friction: 0.6=μN=μ×1.2, solving gives μ=0.5. After the magnetic field is reversed, the direction of the Ampere force is reversed as a whole: the direction of the component along the guide rails is reversed, and the vertical component becomes downward, therefore the support force increases. Let the magnetic induction intensity at this time be B, then the magnitude of the Ampere force is BIL=B×1×0.5=0.5B. The component along the guide rails is 0.5B sin37°=0.5B×0.6=0.3B; the vertically downward component is 0.5B cos37°=0.5B×0.8=0.4B. Therefore N=mg+0.4B=2+0.4B. When the rod is just about to move, the maximum static friction equals the sliding friction, so 0.3B=μN=0.5(2+0.4B). Solving gives 0.3B=1+0.2B, 0.1B=1, so B=10 T. Final answer: μ=0.5; after the magnetic field is reversed, when it just begins to move, B=10 T.
